rows.rationale: Road locomotives were specifically constrained, but no mature vehicle-approval, liability, infrastructure or international-recognition architecture had formed.
rows.caveat: Liability and infrastructure coding is based on absence of demonstrated technology-specific integration, not absence of general law.

rows.rationale: The law intensified operating and crew constraints while other regulatory layers remained largely unintegrated.
rows.caveat: Do not equate restrictive regulation with low regulatory activity: N1 denotes bounded accommodation, not deregulation.

rows.rationale: Operational rules were recalibrated and infrastructure/bridge concerns received more structured treatment, while vehicle approval, liability and international layers remained immature.
rows.caveat: Infrastructure is coded N1 because the regime reacts to roads/bridges but does not yet evidence system-wide infrastructural institutionalisation.

rows.rationale: Reclassification and deeming integrate the technology into inherited carriage law without yet producing mature liability, infrastructure or international layers.
rows.bridge: Classificatory bridge: light locomotive ‘deemed to be a carriage’
rows.caveat: N2 does not imply comprehensive motor-vehicle law; it denotes transitional/intermediate integration. The classificatory bridge is coded separately as the mechanism supporting that state.

rows.rationale: Operation, driver identity and behavioural governance become dedicated and stable before liability, infrastructure and international recognition catch up.
rows.caveat: Driver licensing was initially identification-oriented rather than a mature competence-testing regime; N3 reflects dedicated legal institutionalisation, not full substantive maturity.

rows.regime_label: 1926 · International Convention relative to Motor Traffic
rows.rationale: Approved type/vehicle examination, driver authorisation and international certificate recognition are institutionalised, while liability and infrastructure remain less converged.
rows.caveat: The liability score reflects the UK/European motor-risk environment rather than obligations created by the 1926 Convention itself.

rows.rationale: Road operation, driver conduct, compulsory third-party insurance and enforcement are routinised within a mature system of automobility; technical/infrastructure/international layers remain highly institutionalised but not coded as fully routinised.
rows.caveat: N4 is not deregulation: the mature system is more institutionally dense than the 1865 regime.

rows.regime_label: 2018 · EU type-approval baseline + Vienna/WP.29 bridge architecture
rows.rationale: EU law can accommodate new vehicle technologies through type-approval exception/equivalence mechanisms, but full-ADS operational and actor layers remain largely national or inherited.
rows.caveat: 2018 is used as an analytical baseline; Regulation 2018/858 applied later and the score reflects the emerging architecture rather than one single commencement date.

rows.regime_label: 2022 · EU ADS type approval + Vienna Convention Article 34bis
rows.rationale: Dedicated ADS type-approval requirements reach N3 while Article 34bis bridges the driver requirement only where both technical rules and domestic operating law are satisfied; operation and actor allocation therefore remain less normalised.
rows.caveat: Article 34bis entered into force on 14 July 2022; it does not designate the ADS as the legal driver and does not create uniform domestic operational law.

rows.regime_label: 2026 · Consolidated EU ADS type approval + new UNECE ADS Regulation/GTR
rows.rationale: Technical and international ADS regulation is comparatively mature, including the June 2026 UNECE ADS instruments, while road operation, actor allocation and infrastructure remain more fragmented. EU 2026/481 moves automated parking toward unlimited-series market access.
rows.bridge: Dedicated technical harmonisation + persistent operational bridges
rows.caveat: Technical approval is coded N3 overall because N4-like unlimited-series treatment currently applies to a narrower automated-parking sublayer, not to all ADS deployment.

rows.rationale: The Act creates dedicated self-driving authorisation, ASDE and NUiC operator roles and reallocates responsibility, while full operational use depends on subsequent safety principles and implementation measures.
rows.caveat: Scores distinguish enacted legal architecture from operational commencement; the principal authorisation scheme was not yet fully deployable in 2024.

rows.regime_label: 2026 · Pre-full-implementation phase: passenger permits + draft safety principles
rows.rationale: Actor and responsibility architecture is already dedicated, but the full authorisation regime is planned for 2027; 2026 passenger-service permits and trialling provide conditional operational pathways while the Statement of Safety Principles is still being finalised.
rows.caveat: Automated passenger services are more mature than the general authorisation layer; the row codes the overall GB regime rather than the most advanced sub-use-case.

findings_table.Empirical implication: Operation, driver/actor and behavioural rules reach N3 while liability/infrastructure/international recognition remain N0–N1.
findings_table.Article use: Strong evidence that normalisation is not one transition; the regulatory system can be highly developed in some functions and rudimentary in others.

findings_table.Empirical implication: The layer range narrows as liability/risk pooling and system-level road governance catch up.
findings_table.Article use: Supports defining normalisation as convergence toward stable embedding, not deregulation.

findings_table.Empirical implication: Technical approval and international harmonisation are N3 while operation, actors and infrastructure remain N1–N2.
findings_table.Article use: Direct empirical support for layered/asynchronous normalisation and the dual-pillar claim.

findings_table.Finding: Great Britain shows law can lead implementation
findings_table.Empirical implication: Dedicated actors and responsibility rules reach N3 before full operational authorisation and final safety principles are in force.
findings_table.Article use: Important falsification of a simplistic pacing problem: asynchrony is multidirectional, not merely technology-fast/law-slow.

findings_table.Finding: Legal bridges cluster in high-asymmetry periods
findings_table.Empirical implication: 1896 reclassification, EU Article 39, Article 34bis and UK passenger permits appear where one layer needs to function before adjacent layers are fully institutionalised.
findings_table.Article use: Supports treating legal bridges as mechanisms for managing inter-layer mismatch rather than as isolated drafting techniques.

purpose: Empirical Test v1 – Layered / Asynchronous Regulatory Normalisation

Coding principle: N0–N4 measures the degree of legal embedding of the technology in each functional regulatory layer, not regulatory intensity. Scores are ordinal and heuristic. N2 denotes transitional/intermediate integration and is coded independently of the bridge or gate mechanism identified in column M. The range (max–min) is used only as a descriptive signal of inter-layer asymmetry, not as a statistical index.
